{{Short description|Fundamental topographical problem}}
[[File:HansenPblm1.svg|350px|right]]

In [[trigonometry]], '''Hansen's problem''' is a problem in planar [[surveying]], named after the astronomer [[Peter Andreas Hansen]] (1795&ndash;1874), who worked on the [[geodetic survey of Denmark]]. There are two known points {{mvar|A, B}}, and two unknown points {{math|''P''<sub>1</sub>, ''P''<sub>2</sub>}}. From {{math|''P''<sub>1</sub>}} and {{math|''P''<sub>2</sub>}} an observer measures the angles made by the lines of sight to each of the other three points.  The problem is to find the positions of {{math|''P''<sub>1</sub>}} and {{math|''P''<sub>2</sub>}}. See figure; the angles measured are&nbsp;{{math|(''&alpha;''<sub>1</sub>, ''&beta;''<sub>1</sub>, ''&alpha;''<sub>2</sub>, ''&beta;''<sub>2</sub>)}}.

Since it involves observations of angles made at unknown points, the problem is an example of [[Resection (orientation)|resection]] (as opposed to intersection).

== Solution method overview==

Define the following angles:
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{5}
  \gamma &= \angle P_1 AP_2, &\quad \delta &= \angle P_1BP_2, \\[4pt]
  \phi &= \angle P_2 AB, &\quad \psi &= \angle P_1 BA. 
\end{alignat}</math>
As a first step we will solve for {{mvar|&phi;}} and {{mvar|&psi;}}.
The sum of these two unknown angles is equal to the sum of {{math|''&beta;''<sub>1</sub>}} and {{math|''&beta;''<sub>2</sub>}}, yielding the equation

<math display=block>\phi + \psi = \beta_1 + \beta_2.</math>

A second equation can be found more laboriously, as follows.  The [[law of sines]] yields

<math display=block>
  \frac{\overline{AB}}{\overline{P_2 B}} = \frac{\sin \alpha_2}{\sin \phi}, \qquad 
  \frac{\overline{P_2 B}}{\overline{P_1 P_2}} = \frac{\sin \beta_1}{\sin \delta}.
</math>

Combining these, we get

<math display=block>
  \frac{\overline{AB}}{\overline{P_1 P_2}} = \frac{\sin \alpha_2 \sin \beta_1}{\sin \phi \sin \delta}.</math>

Entirely analogous reasoning on the other side yields

<math display=block>
  \frac{\overline{AB}}{\overline{P_1 P_2}} = \frac{\sin \alpha_1 \sin \beta_2}{\sin \psi \sin \gamma}.</math>

Setting these two equal gives

<math display=block>
  \frac{\sin \phi}{\sin \psi} = \frac{\sin \gamma \sin \alpha_2 \sin \beta_1}{\sin \delta \sin \alpha_1 \sin \beta_2} = k.</math>

Using a known [[trigonometric identity]] this ratio of sines can be expressed as the tangent of an angle difference:

:<math>\tan \tfrac12(\phi - \psi) = \frac{k-1}{k+1} \tan\tfrac12(\phi + \psi).</math>  

Where <math>k = \frac{\sin \phi}{\sin \psi}.</math>

This is the second equation we need. Once we solve the two equations for the two unknowns {{mvar|&phi;, &psi;}}, we can use either of the two expressions above for <math>\tfrac{\overline{AB}}{\overline{P_1 P_2}}</math> to find {{tmath|\overline{P_1P_2} }} since {{overline|{{mvar|AB}}}} is known.  We can then find all the other segments using the law of sines.<ref>Udo Hebisch: Ebene und Sphaerische Trigonometrie, Kapitel 1, Beispiel 4 (2005, 2006)[http://www.mathe.tu-freiberg.de/~hebisch/skripte/sphaerik/strigo.pdf] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160222064142/http://www.mathe.tu-freiberg.de/~hebisch/skripte/sphaerik/strigo.pdf|date=2016-02-22}}</ref>

== Solution algorithm ==
We are given four angles {{math|(''α''<sub>1</sub>,&nbsp;''β''<sub>1</sub>,&nbsp;''α''<sub>2</sub>,&nbsp;''β''<sub>2</sub>)}} and the distance {{overline|{{mvar|AB}}}}.  The calculation proceeds as follows:

* Calculate <math display=block>\begin{align}
  \gamma &= \pi-\alpha_1-\beta_1-\beta_2, \\
  \delta &= \pi-\alpha_2-\beta_1-\beta_2.
\end{align}</math>
* Calculate <math display=block>
  k = \frac{\sin \gamma \sin \alpha_2 \sin \beta_1}{\sin \delta \sin \alpha_1 \sin \beta_2}.
</math>
* Let <math display=block> 
  s = \beta_1+\beta_2, \quad 
  d = 2 \arctan \left( \frac{k-1}{k+1} \tan\tfrac12 s \right)
</math> and then <math display=block>
  \phi = \frac{s+d}{2}, \quad 
  \psi = \frac{s-d}{2}.
</math>

Calculate <math display="block">\overline{P_1 P_2} = \overline{AB} \ \frac{\sin \phi \sin \delta}{\sin \alpha_2 \sin \beta_1}
</math> or equivalently <math display="block">
  \overline{P_1 P_2} = \overline{AB} \  \frac{\sin \psi \sin \gamma}{\sin \alpha_1 \sin \beta_2}.
</math> If one of these fractions has a denominator close to zero, use the other one.
